Introduction:

      Molecular biology techniques are applicable not only to modern medical practice but
      also to the identification of genetically modified organisms, forensics, and quality
      assessment of laboratory animals, pharmacogenomics, and other fields.
      This procedure manual encompasses most widely used molecular biology techniques namely
      DNA extraction, end-point and Real-Time PCR.

Safety Considerations:

   ❖ Use personal protective equipment such as disposable gloves, lab coats, disposable masks,
     etc.
   ❖ Handle all sharps with care and dispose of sharps in the sharp’s disposal containers.
   ❖ Handle hazardous chemicals and samples carefully. Blood and other body fluid must be
     considered potentially hazardous. Biological waste should be disposed of in the designated
     trash bags that could be incinerated later on.
   ❖ Decontaminate the work benches regularly and especially before and after work. For
     decontamination, wipe the surfaces with 10% bleach followed by water.

Minimum Standards and Controls:
   ❖ During DNA extraction, PCR and other experiments appropriate standards and controls should
     be used to assure the quality of the results.
   ❖ Positive control to check the efficiency of the reagents, procedure and equipment.
   ❖ Negative Control to check the contamination

Validation of Critical Reagents and Procedures:

      All technical procedures and critical reagents should be tested and validated before
      performing the actual case work or research work experiments.

Calibration of Instruments:

      All instruments should be calibrated according to required schedule and before
      performing the validation studies, case work and research experiments

Practical 01:
Preparation of Slides (Dry Mount)
Making microscopic slides is a great skill. The first step in making Microscopic slides is to choose the type
of mount. The "mount" is simply the way in which a specimen is placed on the slide.

When we are making microscopic slides there are three types of mounts we can Prepare. These are
wet mount, dry mount, and prepared mount. Each mount has its own Pros and cons.

Dry Mount Microscope Slides:

Instructions:

Dry mounts microscope slides are the easiest to make.

Material:

        •   Glass slide
        •   Cover slips.

Dry mounts work best for samples like:

        •   Pollen
        •   Hair
        •   Feathers
        •   Or even dust particles caught in a microfilm filter.

Steps to Make Dry mount Slides:

The basic steps to Make dry mount slides are very simple. Place the sample on the slide and cover.
The cover will protect both your sample and lenses (Objective).

Note:
These mounts are temporary unless you seal the cover slip in some way. It is harder to see the more
complex structures of some species. For that reason, you will have to learn how to make a prepared
mount.

Practical 02:
Preparation of Slides (Wet Mount):
Instructions:

       Wet mount microscopic slides have a lot of advantages. To see intricate structures the
       liquid refraction makes it much easier. The specimen is viewable in both the natural color
       and mobility patterns if the specimen is alive.

Procedure to Make Wet Mount Microscope Slides:

To make wet mount,

       1. Place a few drops of your desired liquid on the slide.

       2. Add the specimen to your liquid.

       3. Then place a few more drops on top of it. This ensures that the specimen will be
          covered in the liquid.

   Looking at an aquatic specimen like algae, use the water in which the specimen is exist in.

       4. Next apply the cover slip. This is done very softly in order to avoid the formation of air
          bubbles. Slowly lower the cover down at an angle, and it will ultimately be held in
          place by surface tension. If the cover slip is instable on the bottom half of the slide, you
          have used too much liquid.
          There are a variety of liquids that are suitable for making a wet mount, from tap water
          to glycerin. The important thing to consider is your type of sample. Some samples don’t
          do well when faced with certain liquids. Be sure to choose your liquid sensibly to match
          your sample.

          Note:
          Wet mounts have weaknesses as well. Finding a moving specimen can be a problem.

    Lesson 41: Separation Techniques
    Some are the benefits of separating mixtures
   Have a drinking water.
   Segregation of non-biodegradable to biodegaradable wastes.
   Separating mixtures in mining gold copper and other minerals.
   Cleaning oil spills.
   Separating sand from rocks in construction.

    Why is separation important?
    Separation of substances is necessary to obtain pure substances for domestic purposes,
    industrial purposes and research work. Even the example used earlier of gases present in air is
    also an example of obtaining pure substances.

    How many separation techniques are there?
    A mixture is composed of two or more types of matter that can be present in varying amounts
    and can be physically separated by using methods that use physical properties to separate the
    components of the mixture, such as evaporation, distillation, filtration and chromatography.

    Can a pure substance be separated?

    The prime difference lies in the fact that pure substances cannot be physically separated while
    mixtures can be. ... A pure substance, any compound or element, can't be separated into
    different atoms by physical methods. A chemical reaction must occur to separate a compound
    into its different atoms/elements.

    How Decanting Works

    Decanting is done to separate particulates from a liquid by allowing the solids to settle to the
    bottom of the mixture and pouring off the particle-free part of the liquid.

    Examples of Decantation

    For example, a mixture (possibly from a precipitation reaction) is allowed to stand so that
    gravity has time to pull the solid to the bottom of a container. The process is called
    sedimentation.

    Using gravity works only when the solid is less dense than the liquid. Clear water may be
    obtained from mud by simply allowing time for the solids to separate from the water.

    The separation may be enhanced using centrifugation. If a centrifuge is used, the solid may be
    compacted into a pellet, making it possible to pour off the decant with minimal loss of liquid or
    solid.

Lesson 42: Separation Techniques

Separation Techniques
A separation process is a method that converts a mixture or solution of chemical substances into
two or more distinct product mixtures.[1] At least one of results of the separation is enriched in
one or more of the source mixture's constituents. In some cases, a separation may fully divide
the mixture into pure constituents. Separations exploit differences in chemical properties or
physical properties (such as size, shape, mass, density, or chemical affinity) between the
constituents of a mixture.
Processes are often classified according to the particular differences they use to achieve
separation. If no single difference can be used to accomplish the desired separation,
multiple operations can often be combined to achieve the desired end.
With a few exceptions, elements or compounds exist in nature in an impure state. Often these
raw materials must go through a separation before they can be put to productive use, making
separation techniques essential for the modern industrial economy.
The purpose of separation may be analytical, can be used as a lie component in the original
mixture without any attempt to save the fractions, or maybe preparative, i.e. to "prepare"
fractions or samples of the components that can be saved. The separation can be done on a
small scale, effectively a laboratory scale for analytical or preparative purposes, or on a large
scale, effectively an industrial scale for preparative purposes, or on some intermediate scale.

Complete and Incomplete Separation

Types of separation, separations require total purification, as in the electrolysis
refining of bauxite ore for aluminum metal, but a good example of an incomplete separation
technique is oil refining. Crude oil occurs naturally as a mixture of various hydrocarbons and
impurities. The refining process splits this mixture into other, more valuable mixtures such
as natural gas, gasoline and chemical feedstocks, none of which are pure substances, but each
of which must be separated from the raw crude. In both of these cases, a series of separations is
necessary to obtain the desired end products. In the case of oil refining, crude is subjected to a
long series of individual distillation steps, each of which produces a different product or
intermediate.

Sublimation

Sublimation separates a mixture of solids, one of which sublimes. A few substances change
directly, from a solid to vapour on heating without going through the liquid state. This change
is called sublimation. On cooling, water vapour changes back to solid directly.

Iodine is a solid that sublimes. if a mixture of idone and sand is heated in a beaker, the iodine
changes from solid to vapour directly. This is a picture of sublimation process.

The vapour changes back to solid directly on a cold surface. The sand is not affected by the heat
and remains in the beaker. Other substances that sublime include carbon dioxide, anhydrous
iron (III) chloride, anhydrous aluminium chloride and some ammounium compounds. As only a
few solids sublime, this method of separation is limited.

Lesson 43: Filtration

Filtration is a process in which components of a fluid mixture are separated based on their size
during transfer through a porous material. If liquid on one side of a porous material is exposed
to pressure it will start to move through the porous material as long as the pressure on the
opposite side is lower
Functions of Filtration
   • Filtration has many different uses, such as the cleaning of water, like river water, from
     impurities.

                             BIOLOGICAL TECHNIQUES
Lesson 1: Microscopy
Microscopy is the technical field of using microscopes to view samples & objects that cannot be seen
with the unaided eye (objects that are not within the resolution range of the normal eye).
MICROSCOPE: Is an instrument for viewing objects that are too small to be seen by the naked or
unaided eye.
What is microscopy and what is it used for?
Light microscopy is a general term used for any type of microscopy where light is being transmitted
from a source which is on the opposite side of the sample, to the objective lens. Generally, the light is
passed through a condenser to focus it on the sample to have maximum brightness. After the light
has passed through the sample, it goes through the objective lens to magnify the image of the sample
& then to the oculars, where the enlarged image is viewed.

Types of Microscopes
A good microscope should have three properties:
 1. Good resolution: Resolution power refers to the ability to produce separate images of closely
    placed objects so that they can be distinguished as two separate entities. The resolution power
    of:
     The unaided human eye is about 0.2 mm (200 μm)
     The light microscope is about 0.2 μm
     An           electron          microscope            is          about           0.5       nm
     The resolution depends on refractive index. Oil has a higher refractive index than air.
 2. Good contrast: This can be further improved by staining the specimen.
 3. Good magnification: This is achieved by the use of concave lenses.
 History of microscopy
   • MICROSCOPE: Is an instrument for viewing objects that are too small to be seen by the naked
      or unaided eye.
   •   A microscope (Greek: mikron = small and skopein = to look).
   •   MICROSCOPY: The science of investigating small objects using a microscope
   •   1590 - Hans Janssen and his son Zacharias Janssen, developed first microscope.
   •   1609 - Galileo Galilei
   •   1625 – Giovanni Faber coined the name microscope for the compound microscope Galileo
       submitted to the Accademia dei Lincei
   •   1590 - Hans Janssen and his son Zacharias Janssen, developed first microscope.
Parts of microscope
       An eyepiece is that part of an optical system, which is directed to the viewer. It is a
       construction of at least one or more lenses. The function of the eyepiece in a microscope is to
       convert the real- enlarged-intermediate-image from the objective into an enlarged-virtual-
       image. It contains the ocular lens, which the user looks through to see the magnified
       specimen. The ocular lens has a magnification that can range from 5x to 30x, but 10x or 15x
       is the most common setting.
Lens tube The lens tube is connected with the eyepiece and it´s main task is to hold it.
The diopter adjustment
       It is a control knob on your binocular. It is designed to let you compensate for differences
       between your own two eyes. Once you set the diopter, then the two barrels should stay in
       proper relation.
The objective lenses
       It combines with the eyepiece lens to increase magnification levels. Microscopes generally
       feature three or four objective lenses, with magnification levels ranging 4x to 100x.
   •   Objective revolvers are used in microscopes with multiple objective lenses, that have different
       magnification factors.

   •    An objective (lens) is that part of an optical system, which is directed to the object. It´s task is
        to collect the light rays, that are reflected from the observed item. The objective generates a
        real-optical image.
The Microscope Illuminator
  • Microscopes require a light source for viewing. This can come in the form of a built-in, low-
     voltage illuminator light, or a mirror that reflects an external light source like sunlight.
Stage and Stage Clips
   • The stage is a platform for the slides, which hold the specimen. The stage typically has a
      stage clip on either side to hold the slide firmly in place. Some microscopes have a
      mechanical stage, with adjustment knobs that allow for more precise positioning of slides.
Clip
   •    The clip serves as a holder for the object plate and makes sure, that it doesn´t get out of its
        place unintentionally

Lesson 2: MAGNIFICATION, RESOLUTION and PRINCIPLE of a microsope
Types
   •    Depending on the number of lenses, there are two i. e
   1. Simple light microscopes: use a single lens to magnify an object and cannot reach high
      magnification.
   2. Compound light microscope (it has a higher magnification compared to the simple microscope
      because it uses at least two sets of lenses, an objective lens, and an eyepiece).
   •    The lenses are aligned in that, they can be able to bend light for efficient magnification of the
        image.
   •    The simplest microscope of all is a magnifying glass made from a single convex lens, which
        typically magnifies by about 5–10 times.

                                                                                   MUHAMMAD IMRAN        2

   •   Microscopes used in homes, schools, and professional laboratories are actually compound
       microscopes and use at least two lenses to produce a magnified image.
   •   Most compound microscopes can magnify by 10, 20, 40, or 100 times
Magnification
Magnification on a microscope refers to the amount or degree of visual enlargement of an
observed object. Magnification is measured by multiples, such as 2x, 4x and 10x, indicating that
the object is enlarged to twice as big, four times as big or 10 times as big, respectively.

Solution:
Case Study: Filtration in Poliovirus Vaccine Production
Filtration plays a vital role in pharmaceutical manufacturing, particularly in vaccine production. One
significant example is the use of filtration during the inactivated poliovirus vaccine (IPV) production.
This process requires removal of contaminants without compromising the integrity of the viral antigens.

   1.       Background and Importance
The IPV is developed by cultivating poliovirus in cell cultures, followed by chemical inactivation.

The final product must be free from bacteria and particles yet retain the inactivated virus in its active,
antigenic form.

Filtration is a critical step to ensure both safety and effectiveness.

   2.       Pre-Filtration Step
Purpose:
To eliminate large particles such as cell debris.

Method Used:
Depth filters like glass fiber or polypropylene.

Impact:
Prevents clogging of finer membrane filters in the next step and maintains flow efficiency.

   3.       Sterile Filtration Step
Purpose:
Achieve sterility by removing microbial contaminants.

Filtration Type:
0.22-micron membrane filters are used.

Material Selection:
Polyethersulfone (PES): Preferred due to low protein-binding capacity.

Cellulose Acetate: Avoided as it binds to proteins and can reduce antigen quality.

Impact on Outcome:
Preserves the antigen’s structure and immunogenicity.

Ensures the vaccine remains effective and safe.

   4.       Regulatory Significance

Requirement:
Sterile filtration is mandated by regulatory bodies like FDA and EMA.

Validation Includes:
Bacterial challenge tests.

Integrity testing (e.g., bubble point testing).

Impact:
Proper validation helps in product licensing, approval, and large-scale distribution.

   5.        Process Efficiency and Scalability
Proper filter selection enhances process speed and scalability.

Durable, high-quality filters reduce downtime and minimize waste.

Result:
Faster production cycles.

Fewer batch rejections.

Economical large-scale vaccine production.

   6.        Overall Impact of Filtration
Maintains the biological activity of viral antigens.

Ensures sterility without chemical sterilization, which might damage the product.

Supports regulatory compliance and global distribution.

Contributes to cost-efficiency and consistent vaccine supply, especially during mass immunization
drives.

Conclusion
Filtration is a critical quality control step in the production of the poliovirus vaccine. The careful
selection of filtration types and materials ensures that the final product is safe, effective, and compliant
with international standards. This case study highlights how something as simple as the right filter can
significantly influence the success of a life-saving vaccine.

Introduction
 • A cell is the smallest unit of a living thing. A living thing, whether
   made of one cell (like bacteria) or many cells (like a human), is called
   an organism. Thus, cells are the basic building blocks of all

 • Prokaryotic: Only the predominantly single-celled organisms of the

   “before”; -kary- = “nucleus”)

 • Eukaryotic: Cells of animals, plants, fungi, and protists are all
   eukaryotes (eu- = “true”) and have a nucleus.

Components of prokaryotic cells:
• All cells share four key components:

1. Plasma membrane:

• It is an outer covering that separates the cell‘s interior from its
  surrounding environment

2. Cytoplasm

• It consists of the jelly-like cytosol inside the cell, plus the cellular structures
  suspended in it. In eukaryotes, cytoplasm specifically means the region
  outside the nucleus but inside the plasma membrane.

3. DNA
• It is the genetic material of the cell

4. Ribosomes

• These are molecular machines that synthesize
  proteins.

  differ in a number of important ways. A prokaryote is
  a simple, single-celled organism that lacks a nucleus

Cell size

  (μm) in diameter

 Estimating cell size
• Small size, in general, is necessary for all cells, whether prokaryotic or
  eukaryotic.
• Let’s examine why that is so.
• First, we’ll consider the area and volume of a typical cell. Not all cells
  are spherical in shape, but most tend to approximate a sphere.
• You may remember from your high school geometry course that the
  formula for the surface area of a sphere is 4πr2, while the formula for
  its volume is 4πr2/3.
• Thus, as the radius of a cell increases, its surface area increases as the
  square of its radius, but its volume increases as the cube of its radius
  (much more rapidly).

  decreases. This same principle would apply if the cell had the shape of
  a cube.

  increased volume.

Note: Wet mounts may dry out under microscope light. Add extra liquid if needed.

Expected Results: The sample should be visible with clear details, and live specimens may show movement.

### Practical 3: Observation of Wet Mounts of Human Cheek Cells Employing Bright and Dark Field Microscopy

Introduction:
- Observing human cheek cells under a microscope is a simple way to view human cell structure.

Procedure:
1. Swab the inside of your cheek with a toothpick.
2. Place the swab on a slide and add a drop of water.
3. Add methylene blue to stain the cells.
4. Apply a cover slip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
5. Observe under a microscope with X-40 and X-100 magnification.

- Prokaryotic cells: 0.1 to 5.0 micrometers in diameter.

1. Prepare a wet mount slide.
2. Observe human cheek cells under a microscope.
3. Draw the field of view and representative cells.
4. Record magnification, field diameter, estimated number of cells across the field, and individual cell length.

Note: Use microns (1/1000 mm) for measurement accuracy.

The primary objective was to determine whether CRISPR/Cas9 could effectively introduce precise genetic modifications in human embryos, thereby addressing potential therapeutic applications for genetic disorders.

II. Description of the Experimental Design
    • Target Gene(s) and Rationale:
The researchers targeted the β-globin (HBB) gene, specifically the mutation responsible for β-thalassemia, a severe blood disorder. The HBB gene was chosen due to its well-characterized mutation and clinical significance.
    • Type of CRISPR System Used:
The study employed the CRISPR/Cas9 system derived from Streptococcus pyogenes, utilizing single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) designed to target the mutant HBB gene sequence.
    • Delivery Method:
CRISPR/Cas9 components, including Cas9 mRNA and sgRNAs, were introduced into human 3PN zygotes via microinjection.
    • Screening or Validation Methods:
Post-editing, the embryos were cultured to the 8-cell stage. Genomic DNA was then extracted, and the targeted regions were amplified using PCR. III. Critique of the Experimental Design
    • Strengths:
        ◦ Use of Non-Viable Embryos: By utilizing 3PN zygotes, the study navigated ethical concerns associated with editing viable human embryos, allowing preliminary assessment of CRISPR/Cas9 efficacy in a human context.
        ◦ Target Selection: Focusing on the HBB gene mutation provided a clear and clinically relevant objective, given its association with β-thalassemia.
    • Weaknesses:
        ◦ Off-Target Effects: The study reported off-target mutations, indicating a lack of specificity in the CRISPR/Cas9 system used. Comprehensive whole-genome sequencing was not employed, potentially underestimating the extent of off-target activity.

    • Enhanced Specificity:

Conduct assays to confirm that the corrected gene is not only present but also functionally expressed, ensuring the therapeutic relevance of the edits.

1. Phase Contrast Microscopy
Phase contrast microscopy is used to observe transparent specimens like live cells without staining. It converts small differences in light passing through the sample into visible contrast. This helps in studying cell structures and their behavior. It’s commonly used in biology labs for live samples.
2. Limitations of Electron Microscope
Electron microscopes cannot observe live specimens because they require a vacuum. They are expensive, need skilled operators, and involve lengthy sample preparation. They also only produce black-and-white images. Maintenance is complex and costly.
3. Electron Microscope
An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons to produce detailed images of tiny structures. It has much higher magnification and resolution than light microscopes. TEM shows internal structures, while SEM provides surface details. It is used in biology and materials research.
4. Factors Affecting Resolution of Microscope
Resolution depends on the wavelength of light or electrons; shorter wavelengths provide better resolution. Lens quality and numerical aperture (light-gathering ability) are also important. Proper alignment of optical components improves clarity. The medium between the lens and sample, like air or oil, also matters.
5. Simple and Compound Light Microscope
A simple microscope has one lens and is used for basic magnification. A compound microscope uses multiple lenses for higher magnification and better detail. It’s used to study cells, tissues, and microorganisms. Compound microscopes are common in schools and labs.
6. How Phase Contrast Microscope Works
A phase contrast microscope enhances light passing through the specimen, making small differences in light waves visible. This highlights internal structures without staining. It is ideal for studying live cells and their behavior. This method preserves the natural state of the specimen.
7. Common Fixatives in Microscopy
Common fixatives include formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde, ethanol, and methanol. Formaldehyde preserves tissue structure by crosslinking proteins. Glutaraldehyde is ideal for detailed preservation in electron microscopy. Alcohol-based fixatives dehydrate and stabilize the sample.
8. Mechanism of Fixation in Microscopy
Fixation preserves tissues by stabilizing proteins and preventing decay. It works by crosslinking molecules to maintain the natural structure. This ensures that cells and tissues stay intact for microscopic analysis. Fixation prevents enzymatic or bacterial breakdown of the sample.
9. Hot and Cold Filtration
Hot filtration removes impurities from solutions at high temperatures, preventing crystals from forming. Cold filtration is used to separate solid impurities from cooled solutions. Both methods improve purity in chemical processes. Each method is selected based on the substance being filtered.
10. Purpose of Multilayer Filtration
Multilayer filtration removes particles of different sizes using multiple filter layers. It improves the purity of solutions by capturing both large and small impurities. This method is used in water treatment and chemical processes. It ensures thorough filtration.
11. Why Electron-Dense Dye is Used in DNA Visualization
Electron-dense dyes, like uranyl acetate, bind to DNA and increase contrast in electron microscopy. These dyes scatter electrons, making DNA visible. They are essential for studying DNA structure under high magnification. This technique helps observe detailed molecular features.
12. How DNA is Visualized in Gel Electrophoresis
DNA is visualized using fluorescent dyes like ethidium bromide or SYBR Green. These dyes bind to DNA and glow under UV light. The glowing bands represent DNA fragments of different sizes. This method helps analyze DNA in a gel.
13. Factors Affecting DNA Migration in Gel Electrophoresis
The size of DNA fragments affects how fast they move; smaller fragments move faster. The gel concentration determines how easily fragments migrate. Voltage and buffer composition also influence movement. Larger fragments face more resistance.
14. Fluorescence & Light Microscope
A light microscope uses visible light to observe specimens and is suitable for basic imaging. A fluorescence microscope uses fluorescent dyes to highlight specific structures, like proteins or DNA. It provides high contrast and is widely used in biological research.
15. Importance of Gel Concentration in Electrophoresis
Gel concentration determines how easily DNA fragments move through it. Higher concentrations are better for separating small fragments, while lower concentrations are used for larger fragments. This affects the clarity and separation of bands.
16. Vibratome Preferred Over Microtome in Some Cases
A vibratome is preferred for cutting soft tissues or live samples without freezing or embedding. It preserves tissue hydration and reduces structural damage. It’s ideal for neuroscience and live-cell research. Vibratomes avoid the complexities of freezing.
17. Process of Band Formation in Gel During Electrophoresis
DNA fragments move through the gel based on size, with smaller fragments traveling faster. As they migrate, they form distinct bands. These bands are visualized using fluorescent dyes under UV light. The position of the bands indicates fragment size.

Manual microscopy involves direct operation by the user, which can be time-consuming. Automated microscopy uses software to capture and analyze images quickly. Automation provides consistent results and saves time. It is widely used in advanced research labs.

   # Impact of Sequencing Technologies on Agricultural Productivity (1994-
                                  2024)

Sequencing methods and technologies have significantly contributed to agricultural productivity
over the past 30 years. Here's an overview of their key impacts, with references:

1. Crop genome sequencing:
  - Enabled the sequencing of major crop genomes, providing foundational knowledge for crop
improvement programs.
  - The rice genome was one of the first crop genomes sequenced, paving the way for
understanding other cereals (Matsumoto et al., 2005).
  - Complex genomes like wheat were later sequenced, offering insights into crop evolution and
trait improvement (Appels et al., 2018).

2. Marker-assisted selection:
  - Allowed identification of genetic markers linked to desirable traits, accelerating breeding
programs.
  - Molecular markers have been widely used to improve traits like disease resistance and yield
in various crops (Jiang, 2013).

3. Genetic modification:
  - Facilitated precise genetic modifications in crops, enabling the development of improved
varieties.

By M.Kashif(03064963933)                         1

  - Sequencing technologies have supported the creation of genetically modified crops with
enhanced traits, such as Bt cotton resistant to pests (Tabashnik et al., 2013).

4. Pathogen identification and management:
 - Improved diagnosis and characterization of plant pathogens, helping develop targeted disease
management strategies.
 - Next-generation sequencing has revolutionized plant pathogen detection and surveillance
(Massart et al., 2014).

  - Enhanced understanding of soil microbial communities, contributing to more sustainable
agricultural practices.
  - Sequencing has revealed the complexity of soil microbiomes and their role in plant health and
productivity (Fierer, 2017).
